name: The Ship of Theseus
statement: Replace every plank of a ship one at a time, and it is unclear whether the result is the same ship.
meaning: The ship of Theseus is a thought experiment about identity and persistence through change. A ship has its rotting planks replaced one by one until none of the original material remains: is it still the same ship? The puzzle presses on what makes a thing the same thing over time when all its parts are gradually swapped out, and it generalises to any object, organism, or institution that endures while its matter turns over.
mechanism: The paradox works by pitting two plausible criteria of identity against each other. One says a thing stays the same as long as its form, function, and continuity of existence are preserved — so the repaired ship, still sailing, is the same ship. The other says a thing is its matter — so once every plank is new, it is a different ship. Each step of replacement seems too small to change identity, yet the steps sum to total replacement, and our intuitions about sameness pull apart. Hobbes sharpened it: gather the discarded original planks and build a second ship from them, and now two vessels each have a claim to be the original, though they cannot both be it.

examples.text: As Plutarch reports, the Athenians preserved Theseus's ship by removing decayed timbers and replacing them, so philosophers disputed whether it remained the same ship — the original form of the puzzle.
Thomas Hobbes added that if the old removed planks were kept and reassembled into a ship, there would be two ships, and it becomes acute which, if either, is the ship of Theseus.
A folk version: an axe has had its head replaced twice and its handle three times, yet is called the same axe — the same identity-through-replacement puzzle in everyday form.

variants.name: Numerical versus qualitative identity
variants.text: The distinction the paradox turns on: two things can be qualitatively identical (exactly alike) without being numerically identical (one and the same thing), and the question is which kind of sameness the ship keeps.

variants.name: Endurantism and perdurantism
variants.text: Rival metaphysical views of persistence: endurantism holds an object is wholly present at each moment, while perdurantism (four-dimensionalism) holds it is a spacetime worm made of temporal parts — the two give different verdicts on the ship.

whyItMatters: It is the classic puzzle of diachronic identity — how a thing persists through time and change — and a staple of metaphysics. Because everything from human bodies to nations to software persists while its parts are replaced, the paradox forces theories of identity to say what, if anything, makes a thing the same thing across change, and it exposes that our ordinary notion of sameness is less settled than it seems.

working.lead: Separate the two senses of same
working.text: distinguish numerical identity, being one and the same thing, from qualitative identity, being exactly alike, since the paradox trades on running them together.
decide whether sameness tracks continuity of form and function, sameness of matter, or spatiotemporal continuity, since each yields a different verdict.
test any answer against Hobbes's case, where two candidate ships exist at once, which defeats criteria that work for the simple replacement alone.

limits: It is an open philosophical puzzle, not a settled result: different theories of identity give different answers, and there is no consensus on a correct resolution. Its ancient attribution rests on Plutarch's first-century report rather than a surviving earlier source, and the reassembly variant is developed from Hobbes's discussion in the tradition of later commentators. Many philosophers hold that identity may not be all-or-nothing here, or that the question is partly one of linguistic convention rather than deep metaphysical fact, so the paradox may reveal the limits of the concept of identity as much as a fact about ships.
misreadings: It is not a trick with an obvious answer — competent philosophers disagree, and it engages serious theories of persistence. The Heraclitus river saying, that you cannot step into the same river twice, is a related precursor about change but is a distinct puzzle, and its famous wording comes largely through Plato's paraphrase. And the paradox is not merely about ships or words: it targets the general problem of how any persisting thing, including a person, stays itself while its parts change.
origin: Recorded by Plutarch in his 'Life of Theseus' (first century AD), who reports the Athenians' dispute over the preserved ship; the reassembly variant is associated with Thomas Hobbes's discussion in 'De Corpore' (1655), and the underlying theme echoes Heraclitus's earlier remarks on flux.
